mechanisms.name: bidirectional_state_space_model
mechanisms.abstract_function: Process sequential data by propagating state information in both forward and backward directions, enabling context aggregation from both ends with linear computational complexity.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Two independent state-space models run in opposite directions: one forward (from start to end) and one backward (from end to start). Each recursively updates a hidden state using a linear recurrence that mixes information over the entire sequence. The final representation at each position is formed by combining the forward and backward hidden states, thus capturing full bidirectional context without quadratic self-attention.
mechanisms.math_structure: Forward: h_t^f = A h_{t-1}^f + B x_t. Backward: h_t^b = A h_{t+1}^b + B x_t. Output: y_t = C [h_t^f; h_t^b] + D x_t.
mechanisms.consequences: Linear time and memory complexity O(L) vs O(L²) of Transformer. Parameters double compared to a unidirectional SSM. Requires full sequence available (non-causal). Lower empirical sensitivity to input order for unordered data (e.g., tabular rows).
anti_patterns: Not suitable for strictly causal/online inference where future tokens are unavailable.
May leak future information in tasks where sequence order is meaningful and should be left-to-right only.
Simply concatenating forward and backward states without proper normalization may cause feature misalignment.
May overfit on short sequences where full bidirectional context is unnecessary.
Using bidirectional SSM for causal generation tasks (e.g., autoregressive) leaks future information; stacking many bidirectional layers may cause overfitting on short sequences.
Not suitable for strictly causal or real-time streaming tasks without careful masking; may be redundant if the sequence has symmetric dependencies.

mechanisms.name: meta_guided_augmentation
mechanisms.abstract_function: Generates task-adaptive data augmentations by learning a parameterized mapping from input features to augmented views, enabling robust contrastive learning without manual augmentation design.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: A meta-network (e.g., small MLP or generative model) takes the original input (e.g., graph or time series) and outputs augmentation parameters (e.g., node/edge masks, noise scales). These parameters produce tailored augmented views that maximize agreement under a contrastive loss. The meta-network is trained jointly with the encoder, allowing the augmentation to adapt to input-specific distributions, thus improving representation robustness across varying domains.
mechanisms.math_structure: Let x be input, M_θ be meta-network. Augmented view x' = Augment(x; M_θ(x)). Contrastive loss L_cont(x, x') minimizes representation distance between x' and another view. θ and encoder are optimized via gradient descent.
mechanisms.consequences: Increases training complexity due to joint optimization of meta-network and encoder; may introduce instability if meta-network overfits to trivial augmentations; higher memory footprint for storing meta-network parameters.
anti_patterns: Avoid using a fixed or untrained meta-network that degenerates to random augmentation.
Carefully balance meta-network capacity to prevent generating overly similar views that collapse contrastive learning.

mechanisms.name: supra_laplacian_encoding
mechanisms.abstract_function: Unified spatio-temporal positional encoding for sequences of graph snapshots, constructed by forming a multi-layer graph and computing the spectral decomposition of its supra-Laplacian matrix to capture multi-scale structural and temporal dependencies.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Treating temporal snapshots as layers of a multi-layer graph, the supra-Laplacian integrates intra-snapshot connectivity and inter-snapshot node identity links. Its eigenvectors provide a joint spectral embedding where low frequencies correspond to slow-varying global patterns and high frequencies to local or fast-changing details. This embedding serves as positional encoding for transformers, enabling them to attend over space and time without explicit message passing.
mechanisms.math_structure: Given snapshots {A_t ∈ R^{N×N}} for t=1..T, define supra-adjacency matrix Ã of size NT×NT with blocks Ã_{t,t}=A_t, Ã_{t,t+1}=I. Supra-Laplacian L̃ = D̃ - Ã. Use its top-k eigenvectors Φ ∈ R^{NT×k} as positional encoding: PE(v,t) = φ_k(v,t).
mechanisms.consequences: Requires full eigendecomposition of size NT, leading to O((NT)^3) complexity; truncated approximation (e.g., randomized SVD) mitigates but still O(NT * k^2). Memory footprint O(NT*k). Sensitive to node ordering across snapshots; assumes node set is fixed.
anti_patterns: Not applicable when node set changes over time (inductive setting).
Eigendecomposition cost may be prohibitive for large N and T. The encoding is not learned; performance depends on spectral quality.

mechanisms.name: pairwise_cross_attention
mechanisms.abstract_function: Computes a joint representation of a pair of entities by applying cross-attention to their temporal sequences, capturing the evolving interactions between them for tasks like link prediction or relation reasoning.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: For two nodes with temporal embeddings H_i, H_j (each T×d), cross-attention uses one node's query to attend over the other's key-value sequence, producing a context vector that summarizes the relevant history of their interaction. This representation is richer than simple concatenation and can model asymmetric dependencies.
mechanisms.math_structure: For node pair (i,j), compute Q = H_i W_q, K = H_j W_k, V = H_j W_v. Attention scores A = softmax(QK^T/√d). Output = A V, then pooled (e.g., mean or concatenated) to edge embedding e_ij.
mechanisms.consequences: Quadratic in number of node pairs (O(N^2) for dense graphs). Each pair requires O(T^2) attention if full sequences; often done with linear attention or pooling to reduce cost. Does not leverage global graph structure beyond the two nodes.
anti_patterns: May overfit when historical interactions are sparse; need regularization (e.g., dropout).
Not suitable for tasks requiring global context beyond pairwise.

mechanisms.name: self_consistency_learning
mechanisms.abstract_function: Enforce consistency among predictions of overlapping masked regions from different masked views of the same input, improving representation stability and data efficiency.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By regularizing predictions to be invariant to different random masking patterns, the model learns more robust and consistent features, because it reduces variance from masking and encourages the model to capture essential semantics rather than artifact correlations.
mechanisms.math_structure: Given K masked views of the same input, with overlapping masked patches. Compute predictions {p^k} for each view. Minimize consistency loss: L_cons = Σ_{overlap} D(p^i, p^j) where D is KL divergence or MSE.
mechanisms.consequences: Adds moderate computational overhead due to multiple forward passes for different masks; may overly smooth representations if consistency weight is too high.
anti_patterns: Applying to non-overlapping masks without overlap renders consistency meaningless; forcing exact consistency between very high-ratio masks can harm representation quality.

mechanisms.name: residual_decomposition
mechanisms.abstract_function: Iteratively separate a target signal into components by subtracting the part that a model can approximate well, retaining the remaining residual for further processing.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By removing the well-modeled part, the residual becomes a cleaner representation of the unmodeled components, enabling targeted processing.
mechanisms.math_structure: r_t = x_t - f_θ(x_t)
mechanisms.consequences: Increased computational cost due to iterative processing; risk of error accumulation if models are inaccurate.
anti_patterns: Applying residual decomposition without ensuring the model captures a meaningful part of the signal may lead to meaningless residuals.

mechanisms.name: gated_mixture_estimation
mechanisms.abstract_function: Use a learnable gate to estimate the contribution weights of different latent sources in a mixed signal, allowing adaptive combination.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: The gate produces a soft assignment of the signal to different components, enabling the model to dynamically balance the influence of each source.
mechanisms.math_structure: w = σ(Linear(z)); output = w * component_1 + (1-w) * component_2
mechanisms.consequences: Adds extra parameters; gate may collapse to trivial values if not regularized.
anti_patterns: Gate values may become binary and lose nuance if training is unstable.

mechanisms.name: dynamic_graph_attention
mechanisms.abstract_function: Learn the graph structure representing node relationships dynamically from node features using an attention mechanism, rather than using a fixed prior graph.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Attention scores between nodes are computed from their features, producing a weighted adjacency matrix that captures varying dependencies.
mechanisms.math_structure: A_{ij} = softmax( (W_q * h_i) ⋅ (W_k * h_j) / √d )
mechanisms.consequences: Higher computational cost due to pairwise attention; may overfit on small graphs.
anti_patterns: Using static data to learn dynamic graph may cause temporal inconsistency if not properly normalized.

mechanisms.name: mixhop_graph_convolution
mechanisms.abstract_function: Performs graph convolution by aggregating features from multiple hops or distances using a mixing transition matrix, enabling capture of multi-scale neighborhood information.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By using a transition matrix that mixes powers of the adjacency matrix up to a given order, the convolution operation can aggregate information from nodes within k hops simultaneously. This alleviates oversmoothing from deep GCNs and captures both local and distant dependencies.
mechanisms.math_structure: H^{k} = A^{k} (or normalized), then Z = σ(Σ_{k=1}^{K} α_k H^{k} X W_k).
mechanisms.consequences: Increased computation and memory due to multi-hop matrix multiplication; may cause over-smoothing if order too high.
anti_patterns: Using too many hops can lead to feature homogenization across nodes.
Not suitable for extremely sparse graphs where high-order neighborhoods are mostly empty.

mechanisms.name: hypergraph_contrastive_learning
mechanisms.abstract_function: Learns node representations by contrasting the original graph view with a hypergraph view, where hyperedges encode higher-order relationships, encouraging the model to capture long-range and non-local dependencies.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Constructing a hypergraph from multiple relation types (e.g., trajectory co-occurrence, functional similarity) creates additional positive pairs for contrastive learning. The contrastive objective pulls representations of the same node in different views together while pushing distinct nodes apart, enhancing discriminative power.
mechanisms.math_structure: ℒ_contrast = -log (exp(sim(z_i^{G}, z_i^{H})/τ) / Σ_{j≠i} exp(sim(z_i^{G}, z_j^{H})/τ)), where z^G, z^H are node representations from graph and hypergraph encoders.
mechanisms.consequences: Requires careful design of hyperedges to avoid introducing noise; contrastive learning may collapse without proper negative sampling; additional computational cost for hypergraph encoding.
anti_patterns: Using poorly-constructed hyperedges with spurious relations can degrade representation quality.
If hypergraph is too dense, the contrastive task becomes trivial.

mechanisms.name: temporal_mode_regularization
mechanisms.abstract_function: Imposes an auxiliary classification loss to distinguish between different temporal patterns (e.g., weekday vs. weekend traffic), encouraging the model to learn time-aware representations that capture periodic variations.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Adding a linear classifier on top of the learned temporal representation to predict the temporal mode (e.g., weekday/weekend) forces the representation to be predictive of the time context. This regularizes the next-token prediction task and prevents overfitting to homogeneous temporal dynamics.
mechanisms.math_structure: ℒ_reg = CrossEntropy(MLP(h_t), mode_label), where h_t is the hidden state at time t.
mechanisms.consequences: Requires additional ground-truth temporal mode labels (e.g., time-of-day, day-of-week); may introduce bias if mode definitions are coarse.
anti_patterns: Using too coarse mode definitions (e.g., only weekday/weekend) may not capture finer temporal dynamics.
If temporal mode labels are noisy, regularization can hurt performance.

mechanisms.name: rotation_aware_embedding
mechanisms.abstract_function: Encode orientation information into representations to enable rotation-invariant feature learning for arbitrarily oriented objects.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By injecting angular embeddings (e.g., rotary position encoding) into the feature space, the model learns to align representations across different orientations, reducing sensitivity to rotation variations and improving generalization to unseen orientations.
mechanisms.math_structure: Given input feature x and angle θ, apply rotary transformation: f(x, θ) = x ⊙ cos(θ) + rot90(x) ⊙ sin(θ) or similar composition with learnable angular embeddings.
mechanisms.consequences: Slight increase in parameter count and inference cost; requires orientation labels or estimated angles during pre-training; may suppress rotation-invariant features when orientation diversity is low.
anti_patterns: Assumes discrete orientation distribution; ineffective for isotropic or fully symmetric objects.
Can overfit to limited angular supervision if diversity is insufficient.

mechanisms.name: multi_scale_token_prediction
mechanisms.abstract_function: Predict token representations at multiple spatial or temporal scales to capture object scale variations and improve multi-scale representation learning.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By defining prediction targets at different scales (e.g., coarse-to-fine), the model is forced to encode both local details and global context, improving robustness to extreme scale changes.
mechanisms.math_structure: Given input sequence X, define K prediction heads h_s for scales s=1..K; loss = Σ_s ||h_s(Encoder(X)) - Y_s||, where Y_s are target tokens at scale s (e.g., downsampled or upsampled versions).
mechanisms.consequences: Increased training complexity due to multi-objective loss; potential conflicting gradients across scales; requires careful design of target generation (e.g., pooling or interpolation).
anti_patterns: Scale targets that are too similar cause redundancy; too different cause gradient imbalance.
May degrade single-scale performance if not properly weighted.

mechanisms.name: adaptive_graph_learning
mechanisms.abstract_function: Learn a graph adjacency matrix from node features by optimizing pairwise node embeddings, enabling structure discovery without pre-specified topology.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Mapping each node to a learnable embedding vector and computing pairwise similarity (e.g., inner product or MLP) yields a differentiable adjacency matrix. Optimizing this matrix end-to-end via the forecasting objective allows the model to capture latent relational patterns that improve prediction accuracy.
mechanisms.math_structure: A_{ij} = f(\mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{e}_j); \mathbf{e}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d, f \in \{\text{inner product}, \text{MLP}\}
mechanisms.consequences: O(N^2) memory and compute for pairwise similarity; prone to overfitting when data is noisy or nodes are few; requires careful regularization to avoid trivial solutions.
anti_patterns: Learning spurious edges due to noise; using too high embedding dimension leads to overfitting and memory blowup.
May produce disconnected or trivial graphs if learning is unstable; gradient sparsity can hinder optimization; need to ensure no redundant edges.
Learning the graph from noisy or small data may yield spurious edges; need careful regularization.

mechanisms.name: graph_diffusion
mechanisms.abstract_function: Propagate node features across a graph through multiple steps of a diffusion kernel, aggregating information from multi-hop neighbors to capture long-range dependencies.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Applying powers of the graph shift operator (e.g., normalized adjacency or Laplacian) to feature vectors performs iterative message passing. A learnable combination of diffusion steps (e.g., polynomial filters) allows the model to emphasize different ranges of influence, effectively fusing local and distant signals.
mechanisms.math_structure: \mathbf{X}' = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k \mathbf{A}^k \mathbf{X} \quad \text{or} \quad \mathbf{X}' = \mathbf{K} \ast_\mathcal{G} \mathbf{X} \text{ (spectral)}
mechanisms.consequences: Complexity O(K |E|) for sparse graphs but O(K N^2) for dense graphs; deep diffusion may cause over-smoothing; memory scales with K times feature dimension.
anti_patterns: Applying diffusion without adaptive graph leads to fixed topology bias; setting K too large dilutes local information.

mechanisms.name: long_short_term_decomposition
mechanisms.abstract_function: Decompose a time series into long-term patterns and short-term variations to separate dominant trends from high-frequency fluctuations, enabling scale-specific modeling.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Low-pass filtering or multi-scale patching extracts low-frequency trends, while residuals capture high-frequency variations; this decouples components with different temporal scales, allowing each to be processed independently without interference.
mechanisms.math_structure: x = trend + variation, where trend is obtained via moving average, wavelet decomposition, or patch averaging at coarse resolution.
mechanisms.consequences: May introduce phase shift if filters are not causal; adds preprocessing overhead; decomposition reversibility depends on component choice.
anti_patterns: Assuming perfect invertibility without boundary effects
Using a fixed window size ignoring variable periodicity

mechanisms.name: multi_scale_patching
mechanisms.abstract_function: Segment an input sequence into patches of multiple sizes to capture temporal patterns at different resolutions.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By dividing the sequence into patches of varying lengths, each patch size provides a different receptive field; smaller patches capture fine-grained local details, larger patches capture coarse-grained global trends. The multi-scale decomposition enables the model to jointly exploit both short-term and long-term patterns.
mechanisms.math_structure: Given input sequence X ∈ R^(L×D) and a set of patch sizes {p1, p2, ..., pk}, for each scale s, patches are extracted with stride = p_s (non-overlapping) or stride = 1 (overlapping): P_s = {X[t:t+p_s] | t = 0, p_s, 2p_s, ...}.
mechanisms.consequences: Increased parameter count due to multiple patch-size branches; higher computational cost from processing all scales; potential redundancy if scales are too similar.
anti_patterns: Using too many similar patch sizes leads to redundant representations without improving performance.
Non-overlapping patching may discard fine-grained temporal alignment, hurting tasks requiring precise timing.
Using overlapping patches without controlling for information leakage
Treating all scales equally without adaptive weighting

mechanisms.name: exponential_moving_average_teacher
mechanisms.abstract_function: Maintain a teacher network whose parameters are an exponential moving average of the student network's parameters, providing a slowly-updating target for self-distillation to stabilize learning and prevent collapse.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: The EMA teacher yields a consistent, smoother target representation; the student minimizes distance to this target, which regularizes updates and avoids degenerate solutions in self-supervised learning.
mechanisms.math_structure: θ_teacher ← τ * θ_teacher + (1-τ) * θ_student; L = d(student(x), teacher(x')) where d is cosine or MSE.
mechanisms.consequences: Extra memory for teacher network; slower convergence due to lagging update; sensitive to momentum τ (typical 0.99-0.999).
anti_patterns: τ too close to 1 causes teacher to ignore student updates, failing to adapt; τ too small yields no smoothing effect.
Requires careful stop-gradient on teacher to avoid feature collapse.

mechanisms.name: local_coordinate_spatial_encoding
mechanisms.abstract_function: Encode spatial relations of elements relative to each element's own coordinate system, achieving symmetry and generalization across scenes.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By representing each node's features in its own local coordinate system (with position (0,0) and orientation fixed), the model encourages relative reasoning and reduces dependence on global coordinate distribution, improving generalization to unseen scenes and enabling symmetric multi-agent prediction in a single forward pass.
mechanisms.math_structure: For node v, coordinate transformation to (0,0); for each incoming edge (u->v), feature = state of u in v's frame. Update: h_v = Aggregate({ f(u's state in v's frame) | u in N(v) })
mechanisms.consequences: Requires coordinate transformation for each edge (additional computation). Eliminates need for multiple forward passes per ego agent.
anti_patterns: If coordinate transformations are not carefully handled, errors can accumulate; may require careful normalization for numerical stability.

mechanisms.name: heterogeneous_type_specific_parameters
mechanisms.abstract_function: Assign independent sets of parameters to different node and edge types, enabling the model to capture heterogeneous semantics without manual relation sequencing.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By using type-specific parameters (e.g., separate Transformer weights for each node/edge type), the model can learn distinct patterns for different semantic relations and avoid interference from unrelated types, improving representation quality.
mechanisms.math_structure: Let T be set of types. For each type t, learnable parameters W_t. For node v of type t_v, update: h_v = Transformer_t_v(h_v, messages from neighbors with type-dependent parameters W_{t_{edge}}).
mechanisms.consequences: Increases number of parameters linearly with types; may risk overfitting on small datasets. More memory consumption.
anti_patterns: If type definitions are too fine-grained, model becomes parameter-heavy and hard to train; if too coarse, heterogeneity may not be captured.

mechanisms.name: spatial_temporal_identity_embedding
mechanisms.abstract_function: Injects learnable identity vectors for each entity and each periodic temporal pattern to make samples distinguishable along spatial and temporal dimensions.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By adding learnable embeddings that encode the identity of each variable (spatial) and each time slot/day-of-week (temporal) to the input features, the model can differentiate samples that share similar historical values but belong to different entities or time periods. This breaks the indistinguishability bottleneck, enabling simple regressors (e.g., MLPs) to produce distinct forecasts for different spatial-temporal contexts without relying on graph convolutions or complex temporal encoders.
mechanisms.math_structure: Let x[t] ∈ R^C be features at time t. Define spatial embedding E_s ∈ R^{N×D}, day-in-week embedding E_w ∈ R^{7×D}, and time-of-day embedding E_d ∈ R^{N_d×D}. For variable i and time t, the input to the MLP is: h = x[t] + E_s[i] + E_w[day_of_week(t)] + E_d[time_slot(t)], where all terms are broadcast to shape (D).
mechanisms.consequences: Adds O((N + N_d + 7) * D) parameters and embedding table lookups; requires predefining the number of entities (N) and time granularity (N_d); temporal resolution is discretized, may lose continuous-time information.
anti_patterns: If embedding dimension D is too small, identity distinctions may be insufficient to resolve ambiguity, leading to underfitting.
When the number of entities (N) or time slots (N_d) is extremely large, the embedding matrix can become memory-heavy and prone to overfitting.

mechanisms.name: domain_disentangled_representation
mechanisms.abstract_function: Decompose the latent representation space into a shared subspace for cross-domain commonalities and independent subspaces for domain-specific features, enabling the model to capture both invariant and discriminative patterns across domains.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By explicitly partitioning the representation into shared and domain-specific subspaces, the shared subspace is forced to encode domain-invariant knowledge while each domain-specific subspace captures unique patterns. This prevents the accumulation of domain-specific noise in the shared representation and reduces negative transfer during cross-domain learning.
mechanisms.math_structure: Given latent representation z = f(x), partition via projection: z_shared = W_shared ⊙ z, z_domain_i = W_domain_i ⊙ z. Final prediction uses g(z_shared, {z_domain_i}).
mechanisms.consequences: Increased model complexity (more parameters for subspace projections); careful balancing of shared vs. specific learning required to avoid collapse or interference; requires domain labels during training.
anti_patterns: Over-regularization leading to shared subspace being too weak to capture commonalities
Domain-specific subspaces overfitting to noise instead of meaningful patterns

mechanisms.name: domain_adapter
mechanisms.abstract_function: Learnable lightweight modules that act as domain-aware proxies to transform representations from a shared backbone into domain-specific adaptations, aligning cross-domain distributions without retraining the entire model.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Each domain adapter learns a domain-specific shift or scaling of the shared features, effectively bridging the gap between domains. By only updating adapter parameters during adaptation, the model avoids catastrophic forgetting and maintains efficiency.
mechanisms.math_structure: Adapter(x) = x + f_domain(x) where f_domain is a bottleneck MLP (e.g., linear down+up) or scaling/gating mechanism applied to the shared representation.
mechanisms.consequences: Adds small parameter overhead per domain; requires domain identity during training/inference; potential interference if adapters are not properly regularized.
anti_patterns: Adapters overfitting to a single domain's bias, reducing zero-shot generalization
Using too many adapters leading to parameter explosion

mechanisms.name: dynamic_graph_sparsification
mechanisms.abstract_function: Generate a sparse graph that evolves over time by adaptively pruning edges based on local historical information, reducing communication and computational overhead while preserving essential structural dependencies.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: A cross-attention mechanism fuses multi-scale temporal representations (e.g., patch-level long-term and point-level short-term) for each node. These representations are used to compute pairwise similarities, and only top-k connections per node are retained, forming a dynamic sparse adjacency matrix. This local decision eliminates the need for global data exchange, enabling efficient distributed deployment.
mechanisms.math_structure: For each node i: R_i = CrossAttn(H_i_patch, P_i_point); S_ij = similarity(R_i, R_j); A_t = top_k(S) with binary mask M_t; sparse graph G_t = (V, E_t).
mechanisms.consequences: Reduces inter-node communication and computation cost; introduces additional overhead for attention computation; risk of over-sparsification losing critical long-range dependencies; sensitivity to noise in local decision.
anti_patterns: Setting top-k too small may disconnect essential nodes; using raw local data without normalization can cause unstable sparse patterns over time.

mechanisms.name: cosine_similarity_graph_convolution
mechanisms.abstract_function: Performs graph convolution by computing pairwise cosine similarity of node embeddings, achieving linear computational complexity with respect to the number of nodes when combined with appropriate approximations.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Using normalized node embeddings, the cosine similarity matrix serves as an adaptive adjacency weight that avoids explicit O(N^2) dense matrix multiplication. By exploiting the structure of cosine similarity (e.g., low-rank factorization or random feature maps), the convolution can be computed in O(N) time, enabling scalability to large graphs while adapting to changing relational patterns.
mechanisms.math_structure: Let E ∈ R^{N×d} be node embeddings, normalized as Ê = E / ||E||. Adjacency weight A_ij = cos(E_i, E_j) = Ê_i · Ê_j. Graph convolution: H = A X W, where X is node features. Complexity O(N^2) naive, but can be reduced to O(N) via kernel approximation.
mechanisms.consequences: Reduces computational cost from quadratic to linear, enabling deployment on large-scale graphs; relies on linear separability assumption via cosine similarity, which may not capture complex or asymmetric dependencies as well as learned non-linear adjacency.
anti_patterns: Over-smoothing when embedding dimension is too small; cosine similarity assumes symmetric positive relations, failing for directed or antagonistic interactions.

mechanisms.name: stochastic_shared_embedding
mechanisms.abstract_function: Regularizes node embeddings by randomly sharing a portion of the embedding parameters across nodes, reducing overfitting when node embeddings dominate model parameters.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By stochastically masking the per-node embedding assignment and forcing a subset of nodes to share a common embedding during training, the effective number of learnable parameters is reduced. This acts as a form of dropout on the embedding space, preventing the model from memorizing node-specific noise and improving generalization.
mechanisms.math_structure: Given base embeddings E ∈ R^{N×d} and a shared embedding s ∈ R^d, generate final embedding E_final = E ⊙ M + (1−M) ⊙ s_repeat, where M ∈ {0,1}^{N×d} is a random binary mask with sharing probability p (e.g., Bernoulli(p)).
mechanisms.consequences: Decreases parameter count and mitigates overfitting; may dilute node-specific discriminative information if sharing probability is too high; requires careful tuning of sharing rate and mask granularity.
anti_patterns: Excessive sharing removes necessary node identity; incompatible with models relying on unique node signatures (e.g., graph classification with small graphs).

mechanisms.name: content_aware_spatial_decay
mechanisms.abstract_function: Dynamically modulate attention weights by combining content-based similarity with a learned, data-dependent spatial prior, enabling the model to adaptively emphasize or suppress spatial proximity based on local context.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: A gating mechanism computes a decay factor for each pairwise interaction using both the positional distance (e.g., Manhattan distance) and the content representations (e.g., query/key features). This factor is added to the self-attention logits, causing the attention distribution to flexibly consider spatial locality only when beneficial, while ignoring it when content relevance dominates.
mechanisms.math_structure: For query i and key j, attention weight a_ij = softmax( q_i·k_j/√d + g_ij ), where g_ij = σ( W_g [z_i, z_j, d_ij] ) is produced by a content-aware gate over the Manhattan distance d_ij and content projections z_i, z_j.
mechanisms.consequences: Adds a small number of extra parameters and computational overhead due to the gating network; requires careful initialization (e.g., bias toward zero decay) to avoid training instability; may overfit if the gate relies too heavily on content features in low-data regimes.
anti_patterns: Using a fixed, non-learned decay function that ignores content information, which fails to adapt to heterogeneous visual scenes.
Making the gate purely content-based without incorporating spatial distance, which may discard useful spatial inductive biases.

mechanisms.name: multi_resolution_adaptive_graph_learning
mechanisms.abstract_function: Learn dynamic spatial graph structures at multiple resolutions to capture varying levels of granularity in relational dependencies.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By constructing separate adaptive adjacency matrices for each resolution and aggregating information across scales, the model captures both fine-grained and coarse-grained spatial interactions. This allows it to represent heterogeneous relations that vary with spatial scale.
mechanisms.math_structure:
A_r = softmax(MLP_r(X)) for each resolution r; H = σ(Σ_r Â_r · X · W_r)
where Â_r is normalized adjacency, W_r are learnable weights.
mechanisms.consequences: Increased number of parameters and memory due to multiple resolution-specific graphs; computational cost for multi-scale aggregation; risk of overfitting when scales exceed data support.
anti_patterns: Applying uniform weighting across scales without learning may ignore beneficial multi-resolution interactions.
Using too many resolution scales with limited data can lead to overfitting and instability.

mechanisms.name: difference_attention
mechanisms.abstract_function: Apply self-attention mechanism on finite differences of time series to model temporal variations while reducing sensitivity to non-stationary trends.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By computing attention over the first-order (or higher-order) differences of the input sequence, the model focuses on relative changes rather than absolute values, effectively removing constant offsets and slow trends (e.g., baseline wander). This enhances the representation of transient features critical for classification.
mechanisms.math_structure: Δx_t = x_{t+1} - x_t; Attention(Q=Δx·W_Q, K=Δx·W_K, V=Δx·W_V)
mechanisms.consequences: Loss of absolute magnitude information; amplification of high-frequency noise if input is noisy; additional computational cost for computing differences.
anti_patterns: Higher-order differences can amplify noise and may not be beneficial for signals with rich absolute context.
Not suitable when the absolute level or trend is the primary discriminative feature.

mechanisms.name: frequency_domain_convolution
mechanisms.abstract_function: Perform convolution operations in the frequency domain to extract spectral features and capture complementary information from different frequency bands.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By transforming the signal to the frequency domain via FFT, applying learnable filters (e.g., convolution or gating) over the spectrum, and transforming back via IFFT, the model can selectively emphasize or suppress specific frequency components. This captures periodic patterns and separates signal from noise, providing multi-view complementary information.
mechanisms.math_structure: X_f = FFT(X); H_f = Conv(filter, X_f); Y = IFFT(H_f)
mechanisms.consequences: Computational overhead of FFT/IFFT; potential information loss from coarse frequency resolution; need for complex number handling; may not capture non-stationary local patterns well.
anti_patterns: FFT assumes stationarity; signals with rapid local changes may be poorly represented.
Using only magnitude (ignoring phase) can discard important temporal alignment information.

mechanisms.name: retrieval_augmented_enhancement
mechanisms.abstract_function: Enhance model predictions by retrieving and integrating relevant historical patterns from an external memory store based on query similarity.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: The model stores representations of historical data in a memory bank; during inference, a query representation is compared against memory keys via attention; relevant stored values are retrieved and fused with the query, providing fine-grained context that compensates for limited model capacity and captures rare or heterogeneous patterns.
mechanisms.math_structure: Let Q = query, K = memory keys, V = memory values; Output = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) V; often combined with residual connection.
mechanisms.consequences: Requires maintaining and updating a large external memory; retrieval introduces latency and extra computation; performance depends on coverage and quality of stored patterns.
anti_patterns: Using retrieval when the memory store is small or lacks relevant patterns, leading to noise injection.
Ignoring the update strategy of the memory store, causing stale or biased retrieval.

mechanisms.name: decoupled_spatio_temporal_encoding
mechanisms.abstract_function: Decompose input features into separate spatial and temporal representations to model each dimension independently before integration.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By encoding spatial and temporal aspects with dedicated modules, the model reduces interference between the two dimensions, allowing each encoder to specialize in capturing its own patterns (e.g., spatial locality, temporal periodicity). This separation facilitates more accurate modeling of complex dependencies.
mechanisms.math_structure: X ∈ R^{T×N×D} → Z_s = f_s(X) ∈ R^{N×d}, Z_t = f_t(X) ∈ R^{T×d} where f_s and f_t are separate neural networks (e.g., MLPs, GNNs).
mechanisms.consequences: Increases parameter count and may require a subsequent fusion mechanism; potentially loses interaction information if decoupling is too rigid.
anti_patterns: Fully decoupling without any cross-dimension information exchange, leading to loss of spatio-temporal correlation.
Using identical architectures for both encoders when the nature of spatial and temporal patterns differs significantly.

mechanisms.name: graph_state_space_model
mechanisms.abstract_function: A mechanism that models sequential dynamics on graph-structured data by integrating state space updates with graph-based message passing, enabling joint spatial and temporal dependency capture.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Each node maintains a hidden state evolving via a state-space update equation; graph adjacency guides message passing to aggregate neighbor states, allowing spatial relationships to modulate temporal dynamics, which jointly models dependencies across both dimensions.
mechanisms.math_structure: h_t = A h_{t-1} + B x_t;  h_t^{(i)} = f( h_t^{(i)} + sum_{j in N(i)} W e_{ji} * h_t^{(j)} )  (with optional SSM per node, and graph convolution in state transition)
mechanisms.consequences: Higher memory and computation cost compared to standard SSM due to adjacency processing; sensitive to graph structure quality and sparsity.
anti_patterns: Applying to dense graphs with O(N^2) edges can cancel SSM's linear-time advantage; naive message passing over poorly learned graphs may introduce noise.

mechanisms.name: 2d_rotary_position_encoding
mechanisms.abstract_function: Encode 2D spatial coordinates into rotational transformations within attention mechanisms, enabling models to capture relative spatial distances and orientation relationships between tokens.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: 2D rotary position encoding applies separate rotation matrices to query and key based on their (x,y) coordinates. The inner product of rotated vectors encodes a position-aware phase shift, making attention weights decay with spatial distance and preserve relative orientation. This allows the transformer to smoothly prioritize spatially close tokens while still attending to distant ones when needed.
mechanisms.math_structure: For token at coordinates (x,y), let R_x = diag(cos(xθ_x), sin(xθ_x), ...) and similarly R_y. Compute q' = R_x R_y q, k' = R_x R_y k. Attention score = q'^T k'. Typically θ_x,θ_y are pre‑defined frequencies.
mechanisms.consequences: Increases parameter count slightly (only the rotation angle frequencies) and adds modest computational cost from the rotation operation. Requires careful design of frequency hyper‑parameters. May struggle with non‑Euclidean or irregular coordinate spaces.
anti_patterns: Using uniform rotation frequencies for data with drastically different spatial scales across dimensions.
Applying without considering boundary effects – tokens near coordinate extremes may alias.

mechanisms.name: memory_retrieval_feedforward_network
mechanisms.abstract_function: Augment the standard feedforward network with a memory bank that dynamically retrieves and fuses relevant historical patterns from past hidden states to improve temporal modeling and long‑range dependency capture.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: The feedforward network maintains a memory bank (e.g., set of past representations). For each current input, it computes a similarity score between the input and memory keys, then uses the weighted sum of memory values as a complementary feature. This injected context helps the model recall recurring temporal structures, reduce error accumulation, and respond to abrupt changes by retrieving analogous historical events.
mechanisms.math_structure: Let h_t be input to FFN. Memory bank M = { (k_i, v_i) }. Compute α_i = softmax( (h_t W_q) · (k_i W_k) ). Then h' = h_t + α_i v_i W_v. Final output = FFN(h').
mechanisms.consequences: Introduces storage overhead for the memory bank and extra attention computation per step. Requires a well‑designed update rule (e.g., FIFO, relevance‑based) to keep memory fresh. May overfit to static patterns if memory is not adaptively replaced.
anti_patterns: Using a fixed memory bank that never updates, leading to catastrophic forgetting of new patterns.
Blindly retrieving from very stale historical states without temporal context gating.

mechanisms.name: low_rank_sampling_graph_attention
mechanisms.abstract_function: Applies low-rank decomposition to attention weights to extract principal components, then samples from the compressed representation to generate a dynamic graph structure for adaptive relational modeling.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Low-rank factorization reduces noise and redundancy in the full attention matrix, focusing on dominant patterns. Sampling from the low-rank space yields a sparse attention vector that defines a dynamic graph, balancing local and global dependencies according to real-time input characteristics.
mechanisms.math_structure: Let A ∈ ℝ^{N×N} be attention scores. Factorize A ≈ UΣV^T (low rank k). Sample attention rows/columns from U,Σ,V to form A_sample ∈ ℝ^{N×N} sparse. Dynamic graph G = adjacency(A_sample). Update: H = σ( A_sample X W ).
mechanisms.consequences: Additional computation for low-rank decomposition; sensitive to rank selection (too low loses information, too high adds noise); sampling introduces stochasticity that may require careful optimization.
anti_patterns: Choosing an inappropriate rank that fails to capture key spatial correlations.
Sampling without proper normalization leading to unstable training.

mechanisms.name: spatial_temporal_graph_autoregression
mechanisms.abstract_function: Performs autoregressive prediction on a dynamically expanding graph where nodes and edges are incrementally added over time, enabling sequential forecasting under irregular and asynchronous observations.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Because the graph expands step by step and the prediction is performed autoregressively, the model can propagate temporal information through evolving node connections even when data timestamps are misaligned, thus bypassing the need for regularly spaced time steps.
mechanisms.math_structure: Let G_t = (V_t, E_t) with V_t = {(i, tau) | tau <= t, i in nodes}. Prediction: f(G_t) -> G_{t+1} via graph autoregression: h_v^{(t+1)} = sigma( sum_{u in N(v)} W * h_u^{(t)} ) with incremental node addition.
mechanisms.consequences: Higher computational cost due to expanding graph size; error accumulation in long autoregressive chains; sensitivity to the similarity metric used for edge construction.
anti_patterns: Applying to dense regular time series may underperform compared to standard RNNs or transformers due to overhead from dynamic graph expansion.
Assuming static edge similarity over time can cause drift when the underlying data distribution changes.

mechanisms.name: context_aware_prompt_encoding
mechanisms.abstract_function: Encode structured domain-specific contextual information into natural language prompts to guide a large language model's reasoning over non-linguistic data.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Extracting and embedding relevant spatiotemporal or structural contexts as text prompts leverages the LLM's pre-trained language understanding to make decisions grounded in the input data, improving adaptability to diverse scenarios.
mechanisms.math_structure: prompt = template + encode(context(data)), where encode maps structured features (e.g., time, location) to descriptive text.
mechanisms.consequences: Requires careful prompt engineering; long prompts may exceed LLM context window; performance depends on LLM's familiarity with the structured-to-text mapping.
anti_patterns: Overly verbose prompts distract the LLM; context noise can mislead reasoning.
Language bias introduced by template wording may cause inconsistent behavior across tasks.

mechanisms.name: test_time_adaptation_via_reconstruction
mechanisms.abstract_function: Adapt a pre-trained model to unseen test distributions by reconstructing its intermediate embeddings using only test data, without modifying the original weights.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: A lightweight reconstructor is trained on the fly to map test embeddings back to a canonical embedding space, aligning the model's output distribution with the expected one; this reduces the effect of covariate shift without retraining the base model.
mechanisms.math_structure: For test sample x_t, compute z = f(x_t) (original embedding), then minimize ||R(z) - z||^2 where R is a small reconstruction network trained on test set embeddings under consistency constraints.
mechanisms.consequences: Adds inference-time computation; may overfit to test noise if regularization is weak; requires a separate reconstruction module that can dynamically adapt.
anti_patterns: Reconstruction alone cannot correct severe label shifts; over-reliance on test data may cause catastrophic forgetting of training distribution.
If test data is extremely scarce, the reconstructor fails to generalize within the test set.

mechanisms.name: hard_negative_symmetric_contrastive_learning
mechanisms.abstract_function: Enhance discriminative representation by constructing fine-grained positive-hard negative pairs and applying a symmetric contrastive loss that balances gradients from positive and negative directions.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: The construction of hard negative pairs (with subtle differences from positives) forces the model to focus on minute semantic features. The symmetric contrastive loss, which treats both directions (anchor-positive vs. anchor-hard_negative and vice versa) equally, prevents gradient imbalance and stabilizes training, leading to sharper decision boundaries between similar classes.
mechanisms.math_structure: L = -log(exp(sim(z_i, z_j)/τ) / (exp(sim(z_i, z_j)/τ) + Σ_{k∈HN} exp(sim(z_i, z_k)/τ) + Σ_{k} exp(sim(z_k, z_i)/τ)), where HN = set of hard negatives, sim = cosine similarity, τ = temperature.
mechanisms.consequences: Requires careful construction of hard negative pairs; may increase training complexity (e.g., dynamic negative mining); sensitive to temperature parameter and choice of similarity metric.
anti_patterns: Hard negatives that are too similar to positives can cause representation collapse (model learns trivial features).
Asymmetric loss treatments (e.g., only penalizing one side) may lead to noisy gradients and unstable convergence.

mechanisms.name: selective_state_space_model
mechanisms.abstract_function: Dynamically gates the state transition and input mappings based on the current input to selectively retain relevant features and suppress noise across long sequences.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Input-dependent matrices A(x_t) and B(x_t) are computed via learned projections of x_t, modulating the recurrent update. This allows the model to ignore irrelevant tokens by attenuating their influence on the hidden state, while amplifying class-relevant patterns. The gating vector aligns with relevant features through gradient descent, achieving feature selection similar to attention but with linear-time recurrence.
mechanisms.math_structure: h_t = A(x_t) h_{t-1} + B(x_t) x_t,  y_t = C h_t,  where A(x_t)=softplus(W_A x_t), B(x_t)=linear_proj(x_t), C is learned.
mechanisms.consequences: Avoids quadratic self-attention cost; linear in sequence length. However, additional parameters for gating networks increase model size, and training dynamics can be sensitive to initializations and gradient stability if gating ranges are not properly bounded.
anti_patterns: Using unbounded activations (e.g., simple linear) for A(x_t) may cause exploding hidden states over long sequences.
Applying the same gating mechanism to every dimension without normalization can lead to vanishing gradients when most gates close.
Overly large delta values cause numerical instability in discretization.
Using unbounded activation for delta (e.g., ReLU) leads to rapid forgetting; softplus or sigmoid is preferred.
Applying without proper normalization can lead to gradient explosion; using in tasks requiring bidirectional context without adaptation.
Directly applying SSM to unordered dimensions (e.g., channels) may introduce sequential bias.
Applying to sequences with strong local stationarity may waste capacity; using naive recurrent implementation (instead of parallel scan) leads to poor GPU utilization.
Applying to tasks with short-range or no sequential structure wastes the selective mechanism; using default discretization without tuning can lead to instability.
Applying on unordered data without a meaningful sequential order may introduce spurious correlations.
Very long sequences may cause state saturation or vanishing gradients if the selective gating is not properly initialized.
Applying to unordered sets without a meaningful sequence may degrade performance.
Applying to non-sequential or unordered data degrades performance; using fixed state transitions (non-selective) fails to handle heterogeneous input patterns.
Applying uniform non-selective SSM where input-dependent gating is absent; using fixed state transition matrices that cannot adapt to varying input contexts.
Not suitable for problems where strict Markovian property is required; may overfit if input-dependent parameters are poorly regularized.
Using vanilla SSM without input-dependency for highly non-stationary sequences leads to poor performance.

mechanisms.name: irregular_spatial_patching
mechanisms.abstract_function: Divide an irregularly distributed point set into patches of approximately equal cardinality but varying spatial extent using a recursive spatial partitioning tree, reducing the number of pairwise interactions for downstream processing.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Recursive spatial partitioning (e.g., KDTree) splits points into leaf nodes with bounded capacity; merging leaves under the same subtree yields patches with similar point counts. This bounds each patch's size to a constant R, reducing full pairwise complexity from O(N^2) to O(N·R) while preserving local adjacency structure.
mechanisms.math_structure: Let P = {p_1,...,p_N} be points. Recursively partition via KDTree until leaf nodes have ≤ C points. Merge sibling leaves into patches {Pa_1,...,Pa_M} where |Pa_j| ≤ R = O(C). Complexity: O(N log N) for tree build, O(N·R) for per-patch operations.
mechanisms.consequences: Introduces overhead of spatial indexing (O(N log N)); may miss long-range interactions between different patches; patch size bound limits maximum receptive field within patch.

evidence.dataset: 大尺度交通图 (万级传感器)
evidence.delta: PatchSTG KDTree 均衡 patch + patch 内深度/跨 patch 广度注意力交替, 大尺度图约 10× 提速

anti_patterns: Applying to data with strong global correlations may underperform because patch isolation blocks inter-patch interactions at the patching level.
Overly large patch size (high R) defeats complexity reduction; overly small patches lose local structure.

mechanisms.name: depth_breadth_attention
mechanisms.abstract_function: Apply hierarchical attention over a set of patches: local self-attention within each patch (depth) and global cross-attention across patches using corresponding-index tokens (breadth), capturing multi-scale dependencies efficiently.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Depth attention computes pairwise dot-product among all points within the same patch, modeling fine-grained local interactions (complexity O(N·R^2) but R small). Breadth attention connects points at the same relative position (index) across all patches, capturing coarse-grained global dependencies with complexity O(M^2·d) where M is number of patches. Together they approximate full spatial attention with reduced cost.
mechanisms.math_structure: For patches {Pa_1..Pa_M}, each with points x_{i,j} (i=patch, j=position). Depth: Attn_depth(i) = softmax( Q_i K_i^T / √d ) V_i, where Q_i,K_i,V_i from points in Pa_i. Breadth: for each index j, Attn_breadth(j) = softmax( Q_{:,j} K_{:,j}^T / √d ) V_{:,j}. Output = combine.
mechanisms.consequences: Computational savings (O(N·R^2 + M^2·d) vs O(N^2·d)); may miss cross-patch interactions between different indices (e.g., index 0 in patch A with index 1 in patch B); requires fixed-size patches to have same number of points (handled by padding in irregular patching).
anti_patterns: Using breadth attention only on aligned indices assumes spatial correspondence across patches, which may not hold if patches have very different point distributions.
Depth attention becomes ineffective when patch size is too small (e.g., ≤ 2 points) as local context is minimal.

mechanisms.name: spatio_temporal_graph_convolution
mechanisms.abstract_function: Simultaneously aggregate spatial neighborhood information and model temporal dependencies on graph-structured data by applying combined graph and temporal convolutions.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Graph convolution captures local spatial correlations among nodes by message passing along edges, while temporal convolution (e.g., 1D causal convolution or gated recurrent units) models sequential dependencies across time steps. Their joint application enables effective encoding of both spatial structure and temporal dynamics.
mechanisms.math_structure: H^{(l+1)} = σ( Λ^{-1/2} Ã Λ^{-1/2} H^{(l)} W^{(l)} ) ⋆ K_t (temporal kernel)  where Ã = A + I, multi-scale or causal temporal filters applied along time dimension.
mechanisms.consequences: High computational cost due to full graph adjacency processing; sensitive to graph quality and temporal window size; may oversmooth for very large graphs.
anti_patterns: Applying temporal convolution without aligning time steps among nodes can miss sync dependencies.
Using static graph Laplacian when the graph structure evolves over time reduces expressiveness.
Coupling spatial and temporal kernels without normalization can cause feature scaling imbalance;
Applying fixed temporal windows on sequences with non-uniform frame rates degrades performance.

mechanisms.name: interpolation_attention
mechanisms.abstract_function: Recover missing values in multivariate sequences by cross-attending to observed variables based on learned correspondences, enabling downstream modeling with incomplete data.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By computing attention weights between missing and normal variables, the mechanism recovers missing values using normal ones. This corrects temporal dependencies within recursive updates, as the model avoids directly modeling missing observations which could introduce incorrect patterns.
mechanisms.math_structure: For each time step t, let M be indices of missing variables and N be normal ones. Compute attention: A = softmax(Q_M * K_N^T), then recover: X_M' = A * V_N, where Q, K, V are linear projections of hidden states.
mechanisms.consequences: Quadratic complexity in number of variables; recovery quality degrades when most variables are missing; may introduce bias if normal variables are not representative.
anti_patterns: Not suitable when no normal variables are available; attention weights may become uninformative if all variables are missing or if normal variables are contaminated.

mechanisms.name: adaptive_graph_convolution
mechanisms.abstract_function: Learn a task-specific graph structure and apply graph convolution to aggregate information among nodes, suitable for modeling unknown or changing relational dependencies.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: The mechanism learns a parameterized adjacency matrix (or attention-based) that defines pairwise relationships. Graph convolution then aggregates neighbor information, enabling the model to exploit spatial correlations even when the true graph is unknown or variable missing distorts it.
mechanisms.math_structure: Let X be node features, A_learned = softmax(MLP(E_i, E_j)) or a learnable matrix. Then H' = σ(A_learned X W), where σ is activation, W is weight.
mechanisms.consequences: Requires learning O(N^2) parameters for A if not parameterized; may suffer from overfitting or unstable graph structures; sensitive to initialization.
anti_patterns: Graph may converge to trivial solutions (e.g., identity or uniform); computational cost scales with graph density; may produce spurious edges with insufficient regularization.

mechanisms.name: heterogeneous_graph_encoding
mechanisms.abstract_function: A graph neural network mechanism that processes graphs with multiple node or edge types, applying type-specific transformations and aggregation functions to integrate heterogeneous relational information into node embeddings.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By assigning distinct parameters to each relation type, the encoder separately models the semantics of different edges, then aggregates messages from all neighbors. This captures cross-type dependencies while preserving type-specific characteristics.
mechanisms.math_structure: h_v^{(l+1)} = σ( ∑_{r∈R} ∑_{u∈N_v^r} W_r h_u^{(l)} ), where R is the set of relation types, N_v^r are neighbors of v under relation r, and W_r is a relation-specific weight matrix.
mechanisms.consequences: Number of parameters scales linearly with the number of relation types; requires explicit type annotations; may overfit with many rare relations.
anti_patterns: Modeling many rare relation types independently leads to parameter explosion and overfitting; ignoring type-specific aggregation when types are highly correlated wastes capacity.

mechanisms.name: latent_diffusion
mechanisms.abstract_function: Generate high-fidelity data by iteratively adding and removing noise in a learned latent space, enabling efficient and high-quality generation while reducing computational cost.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Latent diffusion encodes raw data into a lower-dimensional latent space via a pretrained encoder, then applies forward diffusion (adding noise) and reverse denoising (removing noise) conditioned on input features. The latent representation reduces dimensions, allowing the diffusion process to focus on semantic structure, while the iterative denoising recovers fine details.
mechanisms.math_structure: p(z_T) = N(0,I); p(z_{t-1}|z_t, c) = N(μ_θ(z_t, c, t), Σ_θ); z_0 decoded to data.
mechanisms.consequences: Requires training an autoencoder; generation is slower due to multiple steps; latent space may lose some high-frequency details.
anti_patterns: Latent bottleneck too small leads to information loss; applying diffusion directly on highly structured domains without proper conditioning.

mechanisms.name: linear_attention
mechanisms.abstract_function: Efficient sequence mixing mechanism that reduces quadratic dot-product attention to linear complexity via kernel approximation or associative property of softmax.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By reformulating attention as (Q K^T) V to Q (K^T V) using associative property (or kernel feature maps), linear attention achieves O(N d^2) or O(N d) complexity instead of O(N^2 d), enabling processing of very long sequences at lower cost. This structure retains a weighted aggregation of values by keys, preserving context mixing while removing the quadratic bottleneck.
mechanisms.math_structure: Standard softmax attention: O = Softmax(Q K^T) V. Linear attention: O = Q (K^T V) (with normalized kernel φ(Q) φ(K)^T) yielding O(N d^2) complexity.
mechanisms.consequences: Lower asymptotic complexity but may suffer from approximation quality loss (e.g., softmax kernel approximation degrades expressivity). Requires additional positional encoding to retain order information as the mechanism is permutation-invariant without it.

evidence.delta: STGformer 配核化线性注意力比 STAEformer 快约 100×

anti_patterns: Using raw dot-product without normalization can cause unbounded activations.
Applying to short sequences where quadratic attention is manageable may waste potential expressivity.
Naively applying linear attention without proper normalization can lead to unbounded attention outputs.
Using a low-rank kernel with insufficient rank may not capture fine-grained dependencies.
Using linear attention without any kernel when the task requires highly selective attention over long context.
Ignoring denominator normalization may cause numerical instability in deep stacks.
Using unnormalized feature maps that cause unbounded attention scores
Applying linear attention to tasks with high-precision token interactions where softmax is critical
Using linear attention on short sequences yields no speedup and may underperform standard attention.
Poor kernel choice can cause numerical instability or information loss.

mechanisms.name: graph_attention
mechanisms.abstract_function: Aggregate node features by weighting messages from neighbors via learned attention coefficients, enabling the model to focus on relevant relational information in arbitrary graph-structured data.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Graph Attention computes pairwise attention scores between a central node and its neighbors, normalizes them via softmax, and uses these as weights for a linear transformation of neighbor features. This allows the model to adaptively emphasize or suppress different neighbors, capturing complex dependencies without assuming isotropic influence.
mechanisms.math_structure: Given node i with feature h_i, neighbor set N(i): \( h_i' = \sigma(\sum_{j \in N(i)} \alpha_{ij} \mathbf{W} h_j) \), where \(\alpha_{ij} = \text{softmax}_j(\text{LeakyReLU}(\mathbf{a}^\top[\mathbf{W}h_i \| \mathbf{W}h_j]))\) or \(\alpha_{ij} = \text{softmax}_j((\mathbf{W}_q h_i)^\top (\mathbf{W}_k h_j) / \sqrt{d})\) for Transformer variant.
mechanisms.consequences: Higher computational cost than mean-pooling due to explicit attention computation per edge; may suffer from oversmoothing with many layers; sensitive to graph noise and sparsity.
anti_patterns: Applying graph attention on very dense graphs leads to quadratic cost and diluted attention.
Using single-head attention may fail to capture diverse relational patterns; multi-head helps but increases memory.
Applying full-batch attention on very large graphs may be memory-prohibitive; sampling-based approximations are often needed.
Without multi-head attention or proper regularization, the attention mechanism may converge to uniform weights.
Applying to very dense graphs where attention over all nodes becomes prohibitively expensive; using a single attention head may not capture diverse relational patterns.
May be redundant with simple GCN for homogeneous graphs; attention weights may not be interpretable without constraints.
Struggles with dynamic graph structures.
Attention weights can be unstable if node features are noisy.
Applying to fully connected graphs without sparse attention; using on very large graphs without node sampling.

mechanisms.name: geometric_reordering_scan
mechanisms.abstract_function: Reorder sequence elements according to their spatial or structural coordinates before applying a scan (e.g., SSM or RNN), enhancing local pattern capture by grouping nearby elements contiguously.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Spatial coordinates (e.g., 2D/3D positions) are used to compute a sorted order (e.g., by a space-filling curve or lexicographic sorting). Elements are permuted into this order, so that the subsequent 1D scan treats geometrically close tokens as sequential neighbors, improving local modeling despite the 1D bottleneck.
mechanisms.math_structure: order = argsort(positions, key='multi-resolution curve'); x_ordered = x[order]; out = SSM(x_ordered); restore original order via inverse permutation.
mechanisms.consequences: Adds sorting overhead (O(N log N)); requires meaningful geometric prior; may distort patterns if the ordering contradicts the intrinsic topology.
anti_patterns: If spatial coordinates are inconsistent or noisy, the reordering can break local coherence; not applicable when elements lack a natural geometric layout.

mechanisms.name: bidirectional_state_space_modeling
mechanisms.abstract_function: Process sequential data in both forward and backward directions using a state space model to capture bidirectional temporal dependencies, enhancing the model's ability to infer missing or future values.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Running the SSM forward and backward through the sequence provides each time step with access to both past and future context, improving representation of temporal structure, especially for tasks like imputation that require backward information.
mechanisms.math_structure: Let SSM(·) denote a state space model. Define forward states: h_f[t] = A h_f[t-1] + B x[t]; y_f[t] = C h_f[t]. Backward: compute on reversed sequence x_rev. Combine outputs via y[t] = Linear([y_f[t], y_b[t]]).
mechanisms.consequences: Doubles memory and computation compared to unidirectional SSM; cannot be used online/causal; training may be unstable if forward/backward dynamics differ significantly.
anti_patterns: Using bidirectional SSM for streaming or real-time prediction where only past is available.
Assuming forward and backward dynamics are symmetric may cause overfitting on direction-specific patterns.

mechanisms.name: expert_routing_via_classification
mechanisms.abstract_function: Treats the expert selection in mixture-of-experts as a multi-class classification problem, using pseudo-labels derived from expert performance to train the gating network for improved routing under varying conditions.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Pseudo-labels are generated per input (e.g., best/worst expert based on validation loss); the gating network is trained with a cross-entropy classification loss to predict the optimal expert, complementing the main MoE objective and encouraging correct routing.
mechanisms.math_structure: L_routing = CE(g(x), pseudo_label), where pseudo_label = argmax_i performance_metric_i(x). Combined with standard MoE loss: L_total = L_task + lambda * L_routing.
mechanisms.consequences: Requires computing expert-specific performance metrics for pseudo-label generation, adding computational overhead; quality of pseudo-labels affects routing; may overfit to the pseudo-label heuristic.
anti_patterns: Using inaccurate or noisy pseudo-labels can mislead the gating network, degrading overall MoE performance.
Over-emphasizing the routing loss may neglect the primary task objective.

mechanisms.name: arma_augmented_attention
mechanisms.abstract_function: An attention mechanism that combines autoregressive and moving-average components to decouple and model long-range trends and short-term fluctuations in sequential data.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: The autoregressive part accumulates historical hidden states to capture long-range dependencies (trends), while the moving-average part uses an indirectly generated weight matrix to smooth local prediction errors, modeling short-term fluctuations. Their combination enables the model to handle complex temporal dynamics with both persistent and transient effects, improving forecasting accuracy.
mechanisms.math_structure: y_t = AR_attention(x_{<t}) + MA_attention(epsilon_{<t}; W_ma)  where MA weights W_ma are generated by a lightweight network from learnable parameters, and epsilon_t = y_t - ground_truth.
mechanisms.consequences: Adds minor computational overhead from the MA weight generation network; maintains O(N) complexity if base attention is linear; requires careful initialization and training to ensure proper decoupling; may be sensitive to noise in error estimation.
anti_patterns: If the MA term is too strong, it may over-smooth and eliminate important long-term signals.
Indirect weight generation may produce unstable weights if the generation network is not regularized.

mechanisms.name: parameterized_contrastive_view_generation
mechanisms.abstract_function: Generate pairs of contrastive views by learning a parameterized augmentation strategy that adapts to input data characteristics to enhance robustness of representation learning.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: A learnable augmentation network (parameterized by θ) transforms the input into two or more views via data-dependent operations. By optimizing a contrastive loss (e.g., InfoNCE) that maximizes agreement between views and minimizes agreement with negatives, the generator automatically discovers invariances to noise and distribution shifts, compelling the encoder to produce robust, transferable representations.
mechanisms.math_structure: Let input X, view generator A_θ with parameters θ. Two views: V1 = A_θ(X, seed1), V2 = A_θ(X, seed2). Contrastive loss: L = -log( exp(sim(V1,V2)/τ) / (exp(sim(V1,V2)/τ) + Σ_{neg} exp(sim(V1,Vneg)/τ)) ).
mechanisms.consequences: Increased training cost due to additional learnable parameters for view generation; risk of view collapse if generator produces trivial or identical views; need for careful regularization or architectural constraints.
anti_patterns: If the generator overfits to noise patterns, it may produce views that are not semantically meaningful, reducing downstream performance.
Requires large batch size or memory bank for stable contrastive learning, which is memory-intensive.

mechanisms.name: dynamic_hypergraph_structure_learning
mechanisms.abstract_function: Learn a hypergraph structure from node state representations and perform hypergraph convolution to model non-pairwise high-order relationships.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By dynamically inferring hyperedges based on node states (e.g., similarity or attention), the model can capture time-varying and non-pairwise relationships that static graphs cannot represent. The hypergraph convolution aggregates information across multiple nodes in a hyperedge, enabling high-order interaction modeling, which improves representation for complex relational data.
mechanisms.math_structure: H = f(X; φ)  (dynamic incidence matrix from node embeddings); H^{l+1} = σ(D_v^{-1/2} W H_e D_e^{-1} H^T D_v^{-1/2} H^l Θ)
mechanisms.consequences: Increased computational cost due to dynamic structure learning and hypergraph convolution; risk of overfitting if hypergraph size is large; may require careful regularization.
anti_patterns: If hyperedges are too large or noisy, hypergraph convolution may oversmooth node representations.
Dynamic structure learning without temporal consistency may lead to unstable hypergraphs across time steps.

mechanisms.name: gated_lipschitz_embedding
mechanisms.abstract_function: A mechanism that produces inductive node representations by adaptively fusing positional, topological, and temporal embeddings through a gated combination of Lipschitz-constrained projections.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By applying a learned gate to concatenated embeddings (positional, topological, temporal), the model can selectively weigh each modality per node, yielding representations that are robust to partial sensing, graph updates, and irregular histories. The Lipschitz constraint ensures stable gradients and bounded sensitivity to input variations, enabling generalization to unseen nodes or changed topologies.
mechanisms.math_structure: h_v = g_v ⊙ (W_e · [p_v; t_v; s_v]),  where g_v = σ(W_g · [p_v; t_v; s_v]), p_v = positional embed, t_v = topological embed, s_v = temporal embed, σ = sigmoid, ⊙ = element-wise product, W_e, W_g are trainable weight matrices, and all projections are constrained to have bounded Lipschitz constant.
mechanisms.consequences: Adds a small number of extra parameters for gating; achieves inductive capability and robustness at the cost of slightly increased training complexity; if gates saturate, expressivity may degrade; requires well-designed multi-modal embeddings to benefit from fusion.
anti_patterns: Using uniform random or non-informative gating may harm performance more than simple concatenation.
If the Lipschitz constraint is too tight, the representation power may be limited, leading to underfitting on complex dynamics.

mechanisms.name: differentiable_mask_sparsification
mechanisms.abstract_function: Learn a sparse binary mask via a differentiable approximation of the L0 norm, enabling gradual pruning of redundant connections during training while retaining gradient flow.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By replacing the non-differentiable L0 penalty with a differentiable surrogate (e.g., hard sigmoid or stretched sigmoid over continuous mask parameters), the mask can be updated via backpropagation, progressively pushing many entries to zero and thus achieving sparsification in a trainable manner.
mechanisms.math_structure: minimize L_orig + λ * Σ σ(log_α_i)  where σ(log_α) is a differentiable relaxation (e.g., hard concrete) of the indicator 1[m_i≠0], and α_i are learnable log-scale parameters.
mechanisms.consequences: Increases training cost due to extra mask parameters and regularization; tuning temperature/penalty is critical to avoid collapse; yields sparse structures at inference, reducing memory and runtime.
anti_patterns: If the temperature is too low, masks may collapse to all-zero or all-one, losing the benefits of sparsity.
The differentiable approximation can introduce variance in gradients, potentially destabilizing training if not carefully annealed.

mechanisms.name: saliency_guided_masking
mechanisms.abstract_function: Guides mask sampling in masked autoencoding by assigning higher masking probability to regions identified as salient (e.g., motion, attention hotspots), forcing the model to reconstruct those regions from spatiotemporal context and learn representations sensitive to task-relevant dynamics.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By masking a higher proportion of salient regions, the model is forced to infer these regions from surrounding context, leading to stronger feature learning of salient patterns. This focuses representation capacity on task-relevant dynamics and reduces the influence of static or irrelevant regions.
mechanisms.math_structure: Let M be the binary mask, S be a saliency map (e.g., motion magnitude). Assign masking probability: p(mask at i) = α * uniform + (1-α) * S_i / sum(S). In practice, allocate a fixed fraction of masked tokens from salient regions and the rest from non-salient regions.
mechanisms.consequences: Requires additional saliency estimation (e.g., optical flow), increasing computational cost; may underfit non-salient regions if saliency guidance is too strong.
anti_patterns: If saliency estimation is inaccurate, the model may learn spurious features; over-aggressive saliency focus can discard global context needed for generalization.

mechanisms.name: graph_masked_attention
mechanisms.abstract_function: Selectively control the receptive field of attention by applying a mask derived from graph structure, enabling the model to focus on local or global spatial dependencies.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: The mask constrains the attention distribution by setting prohibited node interactions to -infinity before softmax, forcing the model to only aggregate information from allowed neighbors. This reduces noise from irrelevant connections and enables simultaneous capture of short-range and long-range dependencies.
mechanisms.math_structure: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax((QK^T)/√d + M) V, where M[i,j] = 0 if allowed, -inf if prohibited (from graph mask).
mechanisms.consequences: Preserves computational tractability by limiting attention to a subset of positions; requires pre-defined or learned mask matrices, adding storage overhead; may become rigid if mask is static and cannot capture dynamic interactions.
anti_patterns: Using a fixed mask that ignores dynamic changes in data can degrade performance in non-stationary environments.
Overly restrictive masks may cut off important long-range interactions that are not captured by the mask.

mechanisms.name: delay_aware_feature_transformation
mechanisms.abstract_function: Explicitly model time delays in information propagation between spatial entities by aligning and fusing features from historical time steps of neighboring nodes.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: By shifting the feature vectors of neighboring nodes along the time axis by a learned or assumed delay, the transformed features capture the lagged effect of one node's state on another. This enables the model to incorporate causal propagation delays in spatio-temporal dynamics.
mechanisms.math_structure: h_i^{(t)} = f( x_i^{(t)}, { g( x_j^{(t - τ_{ij})} ) }_{j ∈ N(i)} ), where τ_{ij} is the delay between nodes i and j, f and g are learnable transformations (e.g., linear projections).
mechanisms.consequences: Improves accuracy in systems with non-instantaneous information flow (e.g., traffic, sensor networks); increases memory and computation cost due to storing and retrieving historical features; delay estimation may be inaccurate if delay varies over time.
anti_patterns: Assuming a uniform delay for all node pairs ignores real-world variability and can miss important interactions.
Using large delays without careful regularization can lead to overfitting on noisy historical patterns.

mechanisms.name: patching
mechanisms.abstract_function: Divide a continuous time series into non-overlapping or overlapping segments (patches), treating each patch as a discrete token to reduce sequence length and facilitate representation learning.
mechanisms.causal_behavior: Patching reduces the number of tokens by grouping neighboring timesteps, enabling transformer-based models to handle longer sequences with lower memory cost while preserving local temporal patterns. It also allows the model to learn patch-level semantic features that capture periodic or trend components.
mechanisms.math_structure: Given input X ∈ R^(L×C), partition into patches of length P with stride S: X_p ∈ R^(N×P×C) where N = floor((L-P)/S)+1. Each patch is linearly projected to a D-dim embedding.
mechanisms.consequences: Trade-off between patch size and information loss: larger patches lose fine-grained timing but reduce sequence length, smaller patches increase computation. Overlapping patches improve coverage but add redundancy.
anti_patterns: Using a fixed patch size ignoring the data's dominant frequency may discard critical short-term fluctuations.
Applying patching without considering overlapping can cause boundary discontinuities if the stride is too large.
Patch size too large ignores local variations and degrades representation quality; patch size too small defeats the purpose of length reduction and increases computational cost.
Choosing patch size too large may obscure local temporal patterns; overlapping patches increase computation without proportional benefit in all tasks.
